h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Indianapolis: Six Days of Preparation, With the Practical Exam Held in Town
html:
Central Indiana makes things, moves things and builds the buildings that hold them, and nearly all of it involves welds someone has to accept. For people in Indianapolis who want the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential, two pieces of good news stand out: the city is one of the places where AWS holds its seminars and practical examinations, and Atlantis NDT's six-day (6-day) CWI exam-prep course can be studied online from anywhere in the state or run at an employer's plant for a group of inspectors. The certification itself comes from AWS, which sets eligibility, administers the three-part exam and issues the credential; Atlantis prepares you and does not grade, see or influence the exam. To price preparation for one person or a crew, send an Indianapolis enquiry.

An AWS practical exam site on your doorstep

The CWI exam splits into three parts, and only one of them forces most candidates to travel. Part A, Fundamentals, with 150 questions, and Part C, the open-book Code Book part with 50 to 65 questions, are computer-based and taken at Prometric test centers. Part B, the Practical, combines 46 questions with hands-on tasks using equipment AWS brings, and AWS gives it only at its own seminar locations. On the AWS list published in November 2026, Indianapolis is one of those locations.

That matters more than it sounds. Candidates in states without a site lose days to travel and have to fit a fixed exam date around flights and hotel stays. An Indianapolis candidate can usually sit the practical without an overnight trip, which makes it easier to get an employer to release you and easier to schedule the computer-based parts around it. AWS still controls the calendar, so check the dates scheduled at the Indianapolis location on aws.org, and remember that for US Part B dates the application deadline falls roughly six weeks before the exam. You need at least 72 percent on each part, scored separately.

Who employs welding inspectors around Indianapolis

The metro and the counties around it support an unusually broad spread of welding work for an inland city. The main sources of inspection jobs are:

  • Powertrain and vehicle manufacturing: central Indiana builds engines, transmissions, aerospace engine components and parts for vehicle assembly plants across the Midwest, with large supplier networks behind them.
  • Motorsport fabrication: the town of Speedway, around the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, is home to race teams, chassis builders and specialist fabrication shops.
  • Life-sciences construction: Boone County, north-west of the city, has seen large pharmaceutical manufacturing construction in recent years, with miles of stainless process piping.
  • Logistics and data buildings: the region's highway network has made it a distribution hub, and steel-framed warehouses and data center buildings keep structural fabricators and erectors busy.
  • Bridges and highways: the Indiana Department of Transportation and local agencies maintain and replace steel bridges across the state.
  • Heavy industry within reach: the steel mills on the Lake Michigan shore in north-west Indiana and power generation across the state draw on the same pool of inspectors.

Each of these sectors uses welding inspection differently, and the sections below look at what a CWI actually does in each one and which Part C code book fits it. A useful habit while reading: note which of these sectors you already work in, because that answer decides your code book, your practical-day focus and the people who can confirm your experience when you apply.

Plant-floor inspection: engines, transmissions and supplier parts

In a production plant, the welding inspector is part of a quality system rather than a jobsite. The work is about catching drift before it becomes scrap: checking that a robotic gas metal arc cell still lays the fillet size the drawing calls for, that a fixture change has not moved the joint off the wire, that porosity is not creeping up because a nozzle or gas supply needs attention, and that destructive cut-and-etch samples are taken and read at the right frequency. Inspectors here spend a lot of time with macro-etch sections, measuring penetration and leg length on cut specimens, which ties directly to the destructive testing and discontinuity topics in Part A.

Automotive and industrial customers usually impose their own weld standards, but those documents often lean on AWS terminology, symbols and acceptance logic. A CWI who understands D1.1 deeply can learn a customer standard quickly, which is why D1.1 is still the practical Part C choice for many plant inspectors. Plants that test welded and forged parts with NDT can read about magnetic particle testing in automotive manufacturing and ultrasonic testing in automotive work.

Race fabrication in Speedway: tube frames and thin sections

Motorsport shops weld thin-wall alloy steel and aluminum tube, brackets and fabricated suspension and safety structures, mostly by gas tungsten arc. Much of that work is governed by series rules and the builder's own specifications rather than a public code, so a race fabricator does not strictly need a CWI. What the credential brings is discipline: consistent visual criteria, a vocabulary engineers and welders share, and the habit of tying every accepted weld to a qualified welder and a documented procedure. Fabricators who move between motorsport and aerospace or defense supply work find that discipline valuable, and the Part A material on metallurgy, heat input and discontinuities applies directly to thin sections where a small undercut is a large fraction of the wall.

Life-sciences construction and stainless process piping

Pharmaceutical plants run on stainless steel piping, vessels and skids, much of it orbital gas tungsten arc welded with an inert gas purge inside the tube. Inspectors on these projects check internal weld profile with borescopes, look for discoloration that signals poor purge, verify alignment and wall-thickness match, and keep weld maps and logs that tie every weld to a welder, a machine program and an inspection result. Owners in this sector expect very complete records, and the documentation habits the CWI examination tests are exactly what a project turnover package demands.

Most process piping in these plants follows ASME B31.3, and its 2024 edition sits on the AWS list of Part C books. For a pipefitter or QC technician whose next few years will be spent on life-sciences construction, preparing with B31.3 makes more sense than defaulting to a structural code. See the B31.3 overview, and for the penetrant testing often used on stainless welds, penetrant testing of stainless steel.

Distribution centers, data halls and the special inspection system

Steel-framed buildings in Indiana are permitted under a state building code based on the model International Building Code, whose special inspection provisions cover structural steel welding on many projects. In practice, the owner engages an inspection agency or testing laboratory, and its welding inspectors verify welder qualifications, fit-up, weld size and visual acceptance for the structural frame, then report to the engineer of record and the building official. CWI is the qualification most inspection agencies expect their structural welding inspectors to hold.

Data center buildings add heavy equipment supports, long-span roofs and large volumes of field welding on tight schedules, and warehouse construction brings repetitive joist, girder and column work where the same errors can repeat across hundreds of connections if no one catches them early. For structural candidates, AWS D1.1 is the obvious Part C book; the D1.1 summary introduces its layout, and magnetic particle inspection of structural steel explains a test frequently ordered on those frames.

INDOT and bridge steel

Bridge work runs on its own code. Highway girders and other primary members fall under AWS D1.5, and candidates can take its 2020 edition, fracture-critical clause included, into Part C. Inspectors at bridge fabricators and consultants checking work for the Indiana Department of Transportation or local bridge owners deal with tighter procedure controls, more qualification testing and more nondestructive testing than in building work. Ultrasonic testing of groove welds in tension is routine on bridge members; ultrasonic weld inspection explains what that test does and does not tell the welding inspector.

Learning the trade: Ivy Tech and the AWS Indiana Section

Ivy Tech Community College lists a welding technology program at its Indianapolis campus, and it is a common starting point for welders who later move into inspection. College coursework can also count toward AWS eligibility: an associate degree in a relevant engineering technology or physical science field lowers the experience requirement to two years, and trade or vocational courses bring it down from the five years asked of a high school graduate to four. Keep transcripts and course records; you will need them for the application.

The local chapter of the American Welding Society is the AWS Indiana Section, part of District 14. Section meetings and events are a practical way to meet working CWIs, ask how local agencies and plants use the credential, and build the contacts who can later confirm your work history. Membership is separate from certification and not required to sit the exam. Because Indianapolis also hosts AWS seminar and practical exam dates, section contacts are often a good source of first-hand advice on how the local Part B day runs, what candidates wished they had practiced, and which gauges are worth getting comfortable with beforehand.

What the six days look like for an Indiana candidate

The course follows one outline whether you study online or your employer hosts it. Studying remotely, you receive the reading, a paced plan, banks of original practice items and an instructor to email whenever a topic will not settle, so preparation bends around rotating shifts. On site, it runs as six consecutive days at the employer's facility, with the practical day built around the employer's own gauges and weld samples. Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad, so on-site delivery means the instructor comes to your plant or yard. Here is how each day connects to Indianapolis work:

1Fundamentals: processes, terms, joint design, welding symbolsReading the symbols on a robotic cell drawing or a warehouse connection detail

3Practical skills for Part BMeasuring fillet legs and undercut on production weldments with your own gauges
4Working in your Part C code bookFinding acceptance criteria in D1.1, D1.5 or B31.3 quickly

6Weak-area review, exam strategy, documents checklistPlanning the Indianapolis Part B date and the Prometric parts around it

Every practice question is original and built to the published body of knowledge, not taken from an AWS paper. The full outline is explained on the national AWS CWI course page.

Requirements AWS checks before you sit

Before any exam date, AWS reviews your eligibility. The experience required depends on schooling: a bachelor's in welding engineering or welding technology needs one year of welding-related work, the relevant associate degree two, engineering or technical coursework toward a welding bachelor's three, trade or vocational courses four, a high school diploma five, eighth-grade schooling nine and less than eighth grade twelve. You also have to pass AWS's vision test. Certification earned now runs for a nine-year cycle; AWS expects paperwork to keep it current twice inside that span, at the three-year and six-year marks, and a fuller recertification as the cycle closes. A deeper look at the rules is in this guide to CWI requirements, and the path beyond CWI is set out in the Senior CWI pathway.

Getting a quote for Indianapolis CWI preparation

Tell us how many people need preparation, whether they will study online or at your site, the Part C code book each expects to choose, and which Indianapolis Part B date you are aiming for. We reply within one business day. AWS lists its current examination and seminar fees on aws.org; the CWI budget planning guide covers the rest of the spend. Request your Indianapolis quote.

Welding inspectors often add NDT method qualifications later, and the difference between the two roles is explained in welding inspector versus NDT technician. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, under which the employer certifies its own NDT personnel; see NDT training in Indianapolis, visual testing in Indianapolis and inspection services in Indiana. faq.q: Can I sit the CWI practical exam in Indianapolis?
faq.a: Indianapolis is on the AWS list of seminar and practical examination locations as of November 2026. Check aws.org for the dates AWS has scheduled there.

faq.q: Where do I take the computer-based CWI parts from Indianapolis?
faq.a: Part A and Part C are delivered by Prometric at proctored test centers, which you book after AWS confirms your application.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run CWI classes in an Indianapolis building?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no Indianapolis classroom; its offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. Candidates study online, or employers have the six days run at their own facility.

faq.q: Which Part C book suits pharmaceutical construction work?
faq.a: ASME B31.3, the process piping code, is the usual fit for stainless process piping in life-sciences plants. AWS offers the 2024 edition for Part C.

faq.q: I inspect welds at an auto supplier. Is D1.1 the right Part C choice?
faq.a: For most plant inspectors, yes. Customer weld standards often borrow AWS terminology and acceptance logic, and D1.1 knowledge transfers well.

faq.q: Does an Ivy Tech welding degree reduce the experience I need?
faq.a: An associate degree in a relevant engineering technology or science field lowers the AWS requirement to two years of experience. Confirm how AWS classifies your specific program when you apply.

faq.q: Can an Indianapolis manufacturer host the six-day course for its inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. The course can be delivered at the employer's facility for a group, using the plant's own gauges and weld samples on the practical day. Ask for a quote.

faq.q: Is there a local AWS chapter in Indianapolis?
faq.a: The AWS Indiana Section, part of District 14, is the local chapter for central Indiana.
